title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 10: Intangible Wealth of Nations
keywords: education and the rule of law
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's December 23, 2007 Inquirer column on the World Bank's 'Wealth of Nations' study, framed by the parable of his cousin 'Kadyo,' a scofflaw taxi driver in Manila who turned scrupulously law-abiding once he emigrated to the United States

The puzzle the parable poses -- why 'the Filipino worker mightily succeed[s]' abroad but not at home -- and the World Bank's answer in the gulf between US per-capita capital ($512,612) and the Philippines' ($19,351)

The study's three kinds of capital -- natural, produced and 'intangible' (human skills, social trust, and the institutions of good governance) -- and the finding that intangible capital is 77 percent of total wealth worldwide

His conclusion that 'the most significant elements of intangible wealth are education and the rule of law,' so the 'much more important focus' than natural resources or infrastructure is 'the primacy of education' and 'the strengthening of our democratic institutions' -- 'the truly lasting legacies'
sub_topics: The scofflaw: CJP's 'distant cousin Kadyo' (Arcadio) drove a Manila taxi recklessly -- running red lights, blocking traffic -- yet 'has never been fined or haled to court'

The three 'L's: Kadyo bragged he escapes sanction by 'lusot' (bluster -- claiming he passed a yellow, not red, light), 'lagay' (bribery -- flashing a hundred-peso bill bearing President Roxas's photo), and 'lakas' (influence -- boasting the mayor is his cousin) -- the 'three Is' that let him 'feed [his] nine children'

Kadyo in America: years later, CJP was 'startled' to find Kadyo driving a cab on the Las Vegas Strip 'so carefully and observing all traffic rules' -- having been petitioned over by his hospital-employed child -- explaining 'I do not use the three Is here because I would... lose my license,' since 'in America, one only needs to be industrious to live comfortably'

The pattern: Kadyo is 'typical of many Filipinos' who 'violate traffic rules here, cheat in paying their taxes... and patronize politicians' but, 'once they are in America... obey all laws' and 'enjoy the blessings of life by just doing their work diligently'

The World Bank's answer: to the puzzle of why Filipinos thrive abroad (the consul general noting they 'earn comparatively more than their counterpart Americans'), the answer lies in the WB 'Wealth of Nations' report -- if US wealth were distributed evenly, 'each person there... would have access to $512,612 in capital, compared to only $19,351 in the Philippines'

Three kinds of capital: the WB distinguishes 'natural capital' (nonrenewable resources, cropland), 'produced capital' (machinery, equipment, infrastructure) and 'intangible capital' -- 'raw labor,' 'human capital' (knowledge and skills), 'social capital' (trust and the ability to work together), and 'the quality of institutions essential to good governance,' such as 'an independent judiciary, clear property rights, effective revenue collection, nonpolitical military, credible elections, and stable rule of law'

The proportions: worldwide, 'natural capital accounts for only 5 percent of total wealth, produced capital for 18 percent, and intangible capital for 77 percent' -- the world average being $90,000, against the Philippines' $19,351; tellingly, resource-poor Singapore ('zero natural capital') reaches $252,607 and Japan $493,241, both on the strength of produced and intangible capital

The conclusion: since 'more than three fourths of the total wealth of the world is intangible,' and 'the most significant elements of intangible wealth are education and the rule of law,' CJP argues that while GMA's 'natural resources and infrastructure priorities... deserve some attention, the much more important focus' is 'the primacy of education, the promotion of the rule of law, and the strengthening of our democratic institutions' -- 'the truly lasting legacies'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's December 23, 2007 Inquirer column, draws on the World Bank's 'Wealth of Nations' study, framed by the parable of his cousin 'Kadyo,' a Manila taxi driver who ran red lights with impunity, escaping every fine through the 'three Is' -- 'lusot' (bluster), 'lagay' (bribery) and 'lakas' (influence). Years later CJP was 'startled' to find Kadyo driving a Las Vegas cab 'so carefully,' obeying every rule lest he 'lose [his] license,' because 'in America, one only needs to be industrious to live comfortably.' Kadyo is 'typical' of Filipinos who flout rules at home but 'obey all laws' abroad -- which poses the puzzle of why the Filipino worker 'mightily succeed[s]' overseas (even out-earning Americans) but not at home. The World Bank's answer is the gulf in per-capita capital: '$512,612' in the US against '$19,351 in the Philippines.' Wealth, the WB says, has three kinds -- 'natural capital' (resources), 'produced capital' (infrastructure), and 'intangible capital' (human skills, social trust, and 'the quality of institutions essential to good governance,' like 'an independent judiciary... credible elections, and stable rule of law') -- and worldwide 'intangible capital [accounts] for 77 percent' of total wealth, which is why resource-poor Singapore ($252,607) and Japan ($493,241) far outstrip the resource-rich Philippines. CJP's conclusion: since 'the most significant elements of intangible wealth are education and the rule of law,' the 'much more important focus' than natural resources or infrastructure is 'the primacy of education, the promotion of the rule of law, and the strengthening of our democratic institutions' -- 'the truly lasting legacies.'
